name: Tool Search and Large Tool Sets
question: How does the agent find the right tool among hundreds?
summary: Loading every tool definition into every prompt stops working past a few dozen tools: the definitions eat the context and similar tools blur together. Instead, keep a handful of frequently used tools loaded, mark the rest as deferred, and give the model a search tool. When it needs a capability it searches, the matching definitions are loaded, and it calls the one it needs. Anthropic’s API offers regex and BM25 tool search, and you can plug in your own, such as embedding search.
useCases: Agents connected to several MCP servers with hundreds of tools
Tool definitions that take more than about 10,000 tokens a turn
A tool library that grows every month

items.detail: sent with every request but hidden from the model until a search finds them (defer_loading)
the 3–5 most used tools stay visible, so common tasks skip the search
regex or BM25 over names and descriptions, or your own embedding search
a few tool references per search, expanded into full definitions
they are the search index: clear names and the words users actually say
right-tool rate, searches that find nothing, tokens per turn and the extra step

steps.title: Start from the whole library
steps.text: Six MCP servers bring 240 tools. Loaded together, their definitions take about 43,000 tokens on every call, and past roughly 30 to 50 tools the model starts picking the wrong one.

steps.title: Keep a few, defer the rest
steps.text: The four tools used in most tasks stay loaded. Every other tool is marked defer_loading. They are still sent with each request, because the API needs them to search, but the model does not see them yet.

steps.title: Add a search tool
steps.text: The BM25 search tool is added once and never deferred. The model now knows it can look for a capability instead of scanning a huge list.

steps.title: The model searches
steps.text: Asked to stop a SIP, the model sees no suitable tool among the four, so it searches: “stop SIP mandate”. That search is one extra step, which is why common tools stay loaded.

steps.title: Matching tools are loaded
steps.text: The search returns references to up to 5 matching tools. The API expands them into full definitions, so only those few are added to the context.

steps.title: Call the tool it found
steps.text: The model calls cancel_sip_mandate with the client and date. Your loop runs it exactly like any other tool; search changed only which tools the model could see.

pros: Hundreds of tools without filling the context
Right-tool rate stays high as the library grows
Fewer definition tokens on every call, so lower cost
New tools become usable just by adding them to the library
cons: An extra search step for tasks whose tool is not kept loaded
Tools with poor names or descriptions are never found
Another moving part to test and monitor
Needs a model and API that support deferred tools, or your own search
avoidWhen: The agent has fewer than about 10 tools (load them all)
Every task uses the same small set of tools (keep them loaded, no search)

practice.scenario: Nivesh Setu, a fictional wealth platform, gives its back-office agent 240 tools from six MCP servers: KYC, payments, portfolios, CRM, ticketing and reports. Loaded together they took 43,000 tokens a call and the agent kept picking look-alike tools. Now four common tools stay loaded, the rest are deferred behind a search tool, and descriptions were rewritten in the words staff actually use, such as "stop SIP" as well as "cancel mandate".

industries.use: Hundreds of order, mandate, KYC and report tools across back-office systems
Separate servers for core banking, cards, loans and complaints, each with dozens of tools
An agent reaching many internal systems, each exposed as its own MCP server

practice.analogy: A big library. You keep a few favourite books on your desk and look the rest up in the catalogue when you need them. A book with a vague title and no summary is never found, however useful it is.

library.name: Anthropic Python SDK
library.what: Mark tools with defer_loading and add a tool search tool, or answer your own search tool with tool_reference blocks, as below.

practice.note: embed() and load_mcp_tool_definitions() stand for your embedding model and tool registry. Every referenced tool must also be in the tools list, usually deferred.

samples.code:
import numpy as np

TOOLS = load_mcp_tool_definitions()          # 240 definitions
vecs = embed([t["name"] + ": " + t["description"] for t in TOOLS])

find_tools = {
    "name": "find_tools",
    "description": ("Search the tool library by what you need to do, in plain words. "
                    "Use it when none of the loaded tools fits. Returns matching tools."),
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                     "properties": {"need": {"type": "string"}},
                     "required": ["need"]}}

def run_find_tools(need: str, k: int = 5):
    scores = vecs @ embed([need])[0]           # cosine if vectors are normalised
    best = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
    return [{"type": "tool_reference", "tool_name": TOOLS[i]["name"]} for i in best]

KEEP = {"get_client", "get_holdings", "create_ticket", "send_message"}
tools = [find_tools] + [{**t, "defer_loading": t["name"] not in KEEP} for t in TOOLS]

# In your tool loop, answer a find_tools call with:
# {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call.id,
#  "content": run_find_tools(**call.input)}

numericDrill.question: An agent has 240 tools whose definitions average 180 tokens each, and it makes 3 model calls per request. How many definition tokens does one request send if every tool is loaded on every call?
numericDrill.answer: 240 × 180 = 43,200 tokens per call × 3 calls = 129,600 tokens per request, before the question, history or any results.

interview.question: Your agent now has 300 tools across several MCP servers and picks the wrong one often. What do you change?
interview.answer: Stop loading every definition. Keep the handful of tools used in most tasks loaded, defer the rest behind a search tool, and rewrite names and descriptions so the words people use find the right tool. Merge look-alike tools where possible, then measure the right-tool rate and the searches that find nothing.

interview.question: What are the trade-offs of tool search?
interview.answer: It saves context and keeps accuracy high as tools grow, but adds a search step when the needed tool is not loaded, and a tool with a poor description may never be found. Keeping common tools loaded limits the extra step; logging failed searches shows which descriptions to fix.

mistakes.mistake: Deferring every tool, including the common ones
mistakes.fix: Keep the 3–5 most used tools loaded so most tasks skip the search
Write descriptions in the words users say, since they are what the search matches

quiz.question: A wealth platform’s agent has 240 tools from six MCP servers, all loaded on every call, and often picks look-alike tools. What is the first fix to try?
options: A larger model
Defer most tools behind a search tool and keep a few common ones loaded
Remove the tool descriptions to save tokens
Raise max_tokens
quiz.explanation: Past a few dozen tools, loading everything hurts accuracy and cost; search lets the model see only what it needs.

quiz.question: Tool definitions for a bank’s agent take 45,000 tokens per call. What does that cost the team on every request?
options: Nothing: definitions are free
Input tokens and context space on every call, before any real work
Only latency on the first call
Only output tokens
quiz.explanation: Definitions are part of the input on every call, so they cost tokens and crowd the context each time.

quiz.question: A team marks every tool, including the search tool, as deferred. What happens?
options: It works the same
The model can see no tools at all, and the request fails
The model loads all tools anyway
Only the first tool is used
quiz.explanation: The search tool, and ideally the few most-used tools, must stay loaded.

quiz.question: Most client requests at a broker use the same 4 tools. How should they be handled with tool search?
options: Defer them like the rest
Keep them loaded, so those requests skip the search step
Remove them
Duplicate them under new names
quiz.explanation: Keeping common tools loaded avoids an extra search step on most requests.

quiz.question: After adding tool search, a claims tool named proc_clm_v2 with the description "claims ops" is never used. Why?
options: The model dislikes version numbers
Its name and description do not contain the words the search matches
Deferred tools cannot be called
The search tool is broken
quiz.explanation: Names and descriptions are the search index; vague ones are never found.

quiz.question: Deferred tools in Anthropic’s API: are their full definitions still sent in the tools list on each request?
options: Yes, so the API can search them and expand the results
No, they are fetched from a registry
Only the names are sent
Only on the first request
quiz.explanation: Deferred tools are still sent; they are just hidden from the model until found.

quiz.question: Which signs suggest a telecom agent needs tool search? Select all that apply.
options: Tool definitions exceed about 10,000 tokens a call
The agent uses 3 tools in total
Tools come from many MCP servers and keep growing
The right-tool rate falls as tools are added
quiz.explanation: Large, growing tool sets and falling accuracy are the signals; three tools need no search.

quiz.question: Staff ask to "stop a refund" but the tool is described only as "reverse settlement instruction". Keyword search rarely finds it. What helps most?
options: A bigger search result limit only
Adding the words people use, such as "stop refund", to the description, or using meaning-based search
Renaming every tool to a number
Removing the tool
quiz.explanation: Matching the words users say, or searching by meaning, lets the right tool be found.

quiz.question: A hospital agent’s common task, booking an appointment, now takes an extra second after tool search was added. What should change?
options: Remove tool search entirely
Keep the booking tool loaded so it never needs a search
Use a slower model
Add more deferred tools
quiz.explanation: Common tools belong in the always-loaded set, so their tasks skip the search step.

quiz.question: A custom tool search built on embeddings must return what to Anthropic’s API?
options: The full tool definitions as text
tool_reference blocks naming the tools, inside a tool_result
A list of URLs
Nothing; it runs the tools itself
quiz.explanation: A custom search answers with tool_reference blocks; the API expands them into definitions.

quiz.question: Two MCP servers both expose a tool for "loan status" with different names. After search finds both, the model picks the wrong one. What is the root fix?
options: A higher search limit
Merge or clearly distinguish the look-alike tools and their descriptions
Defer both
A larger thinking budget
quiz.explanation: Search limits what the model sees; near-duplicate tools still need clearer design.

quiz.question: How should a team check that tool search is working after launch?
options: Count tools only
Track the right-tool rate, searches that return nothing useful, and tokens per call
Check that the search tool is called on every request
Ask the model if it is happy
quiz.explanation: Measure accuracy, failed searches and token savings; failed searches point to descriptions to fix.

quiz.question: An agent has 8 tools totalling 2,000 tokens of definitions. Should it use tool search?
options: Yes, always
No: load them all; search would only add a step
Yes, but defer all 8
Only on weekends
quiz.explanation: Small tool sets are best loaded in full; search pays off with dozens or hundreds of tools.

quiz.question: Which improve how often the right tool is found by keyword search? Select all that apply.
options: Descriptions that say what the tool does and when to use it
The words users actually say, such as "renew policy"
Shorter names made of internal codes
Removing near-duplicate tools
quiz.explanation: Clear descriptions in users’ words and fewer look-alikes improve search; internal codes hurt it.

quiz.question: With 240 tools at 180 tokens each, how many definition tokens per call does loading them all cost?
quiz.explanation: 240 × 180 = 43,200 tokens per call.

quiz.question: A search tool keeps returning 5 tools, but the right one is usually sixth. What could the team try?
options: Lower the limit to 1
Improve that tool’s description or allow a slightly larger result limit
Defer the search tool
Remove descriptions
quiz.explanation: Better descriptions lift the right tool; a slightly larger limit also helps, at some token cost.

quiz.question: A benefits agent grows from 30 to 300 tools over a year as departments add MCP servers. What does tool search make easier?
options: Nothing changes
Adding new tools without growing every prompt or retraining
Removing the need for descriptions
Skipping tests for new tools
quiz.explanation: New tools join the searchable library without bloating each call, though they still need good descriptions and tests.

quiz.question: Which search is better at matching "patient cannot come tomorrow" to a tool described as "reschedule appointment"?
options: Exact regex on the tool name
Meaning-based (embedding) search
Alphabetical order
Random choice
quiz.explanation: Embedding search matches meaning, so different words for the same need still find the tool.

quiz.question: Could a malicious MCP server exploit tool search?
options: No, search is always safe
Yes: a tool description stuffed with popular words could win searches it should not
Only if the model is small
Only with regex search
quiz.explanation: Descriptions drive search results, so vet servers and watch for tools that match everything.

quiz.question: A team is moving 240 tools to tool search. Which steps belong in the rollout? Select all that apply.
options: Measure the right-tool rate before and after on a task set
Keep the most-used tools loaded
Delete all tool descriptions to save tokens
Log searches that find nothing useful
quiz.explanation: Measure, keep common tools loaded and learn from failed searches; descriptions are what makes search work.
